narrative:
The model predicts you have a 57.2% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt—meaning the risk of failure is slightly higher than the chance of passing. This elevated risk is what led to your application denial. Three factors, in order of influence, shaped that decision.

Your undergraduate GPA was the single most important factor, and it worked in your favor. Despite being below the average of 3.23 for accepted students, your 3.10 still nudged the prediction toward passing. This suggests your academic foundation is solid, but alone it was not enough.

Unfortunately, the next two most influential features pushed strongly in the opposite direction. Your LSAT score of 25 is dramatically lower than the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and this carried heavy weight, clearly steering the prediction toward failure. Similarly, your third-year class decile of 2—meaning you ranked near the bottom of your class relative to peers—was the third strongest signal, also pushing toward failure. Accepting students typically land in deciles close to 5.79, so this low ranking raised serious concerns about your ability to handle the rigors of legal study and exam performance.

Even with your GPA providing a modest positive contribution, the combined negative impact of your low LSAT score and poor upper-class performance overwhelmed it, yielding a prediction that you would not pass the bar. To change that outcome, focus intensely on LSAT preparation and retake the exam to raise your score meaningfully. Additionally, if possible, strengthen your academic record in your final year to improve your class standing. Addressing these two areas would substantially alter a future prediction in your favor.
